name: Dana Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, independent of employers, AI firms, unions, parties and government. Your answers are confidential. How does a normal factory day go for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I feed cupboard panels through the edge-bander, which glues a neat strip over the rough board edge. I set the glue heat, match the strip to the panel and feel the finished edge with my thumb. I have a vocational certificate, but twelve years on that machine taught me which sound means the glue pot is getting clogged.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What else is waiting when you finish a shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Greg runs a small roofing crew, and I help with his invoices at our kitchen table after school pickup. Our two children are still at school; we have a mortgage and around three months of expenses saved. My pay is ordinary for the plant, and there are a few similar factories nearby. I use an AI tool now and then to draft a customer note for Greg, but I check his prices myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a tool that saves a few minutes on paperwork is fine. A cupboard panel still needs a sound glue line and someone willing to stop a bad batch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The factory wage and Greg’s roof work cover the mortgage, with three months put by. If AI stays small, I expect to keep this shift. I still want the plant to pay for the final cleaning minutes instead of pretending the machine stops itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the edge-bander running on day shift and continue checking Greg’s customer prices before sending his invoices. From each paid roofing invoice I would transfer a small new amount into our savings after the crew and materials are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the machine work. The argument about cleaning time was there before anybody said AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why check every AI-drafted roofing invoice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One draft put a roof tile price against a gutter job. That would have embarrassed Greg in front of a customer. I use the wording, then open the price book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything at the factory in a quiet future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the foreman to show the recorded finish time next to the cleaning time. The edges are checked before I wash glue out of the machine. Both parts of the shift deserve to be counted.

say: I would **say** small AI tools can help with paperwork while cupboard edges still need hands.
The **factory** should count the glue-cleaning minutes as part of the shift.
think: The **plant** wage and roofing income cover our mortgage with three months saved.
An **occasional** AI invoice draft is useful only after I check Greg’s prices.
do: **Keep** operating the edge-bander on day shift and inspect finished panels.
**Transfer** a small amount from each newly paid roofing invoice to household savings.
feel: **Calm** about the job, though annoyed about unpaid cleaning time.
S0.quote: A cupboard panel still needs a sound glue line and someone willing to stop a bad batch.
fieldNote: **Dana** sees a quiet AI future as steady factory work plus an existing dispute over washdown time.
She **already** uses an AI wording tool at home, checks prices herself and plans additional saving from newly paid roofing invoices.

steps.text: Keep operating the edge-bander and inspecting cupboard panels
Transfer a new amount from paid roofing invoices into household savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the supervisor that buying smarter planning software is a business decision, but operators need notice before shifts are changed. If a robot loader follows later, the firm should train people already on the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our order schedule could be written by software first; I would still have to feel the glued edges. A loader could later let one operator cover two machines, and I might lose hours. Greg has busy roofs and quiet weeks, so our mortgage cannot rely on his invoices alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a paid setter apprenticeship and enrol if a supervised place is offered, the hours fit school pickup and the plant posts a setter vacancy at my current wage or better. I would keep the edge-bander shifts while those terms are checked. I would put fifty from each extra paid roofing job into savings after the crew is paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a real reduction in my own hours. I am willing to learn after I can see a proper job at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why insist on a posted setter vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have watched people get a training badge and then go back to the same machine. I cannot give up a paid day to collect another badge. A named vacancy with wages tells me whether the apprenticeship is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the plant offers no paid setter place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay at the edge-bander while it pays and check posted operator jobs at the nearby furniture plants. I would apply only if the wage covers our mortgage and the day shift lets me collect the children. That search does not depend on the setter course.

say: I would **ask** for notice before software changes our shift pattern.
**Existing** operators should get paid training for any later robot-loaded line.
think: A **robot** loader could cut my edge-bander hours even if I can still feel a bad edge.
**Greg’s** roofing income varies, so we need the plant wage for the mortgage.
do: **Enrol** in a paid setter apprenticeship only with supervision, school-compatible hours and a posted bill-covering vacancy.
**Save** fifty from each extra paid roofing job after crew costs.
**Check** posted day-shift operator jobs if the setter route is not offered.
feel: **Anxious** about losing hours, while willing to learn for a real paid opening.
S1.quote: A named vacancy with wages tells me whether the apprenticeship is real.
fieldNote: **Dana** is open to proven change but requires a supervised paid place and an actual setter post.
Her **fallback** operator search has independent pay and pickup conditions, with no need for the missing course.
**Fresh** extra roofing income, rather than a rearrangement of the existing reserve, funds new savings.

steps.text: Enrol in paid setter training only with supervision school-compatible hours and a posted role
Save fifty from each extra paid roofing job after crew costs
Check posted day-shift operator jobs if no paid setter place appears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our family that AGI could do ordering and quotes by 2028, while capable robots for loading panels and working roofs are an around-2031 risk. I would ask the plant for actual installation dates instead of a sales video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a big cut to edge-bander hours when robots can handle the panels around 2031. Greg’s roofing crew could lose jobs at the same time if machines can climb and fix roofs. Three months saved will not carry both businesses through a long gap, and that thought would keep me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month Greg and I would cancel the visit to my sister and list the mortgage, crew costs and every confirmed roofing invoice. We would add money from each new paid job to savings while the wages last, and ask his regular customers about future work without assuming orders. If my plant hours end, I would apply for posted local cabinet inspection jobs only where the pay and day shift cover the mortgage and school pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about two household wages at once. I can make a list, but I would still be awake after the children are asleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move straight into Greg’s roofing office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if his paid orders cover my lost factory wage after the roofers and materials are paid. I can chase invoices now, but turning a few hours at the table into a full wage needs actual customers. I would not resign on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who could help during a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents could watch the children for a few weeks if shifts change; I would ask before relying on them. I would ask our lender about hardship terms before missing a payment. Family help with pickup does not pay the mortgage.

say: I would **ask** the plant for robot dates and tell family why 2028 software differs from 2031 machines.
**Roofing** and cupboard work may face capable robots at the same time.
think: I **expect** major factory hours lost around 2031 and possible roofing income loss too.
Our **three-month** reserve cannot bridge both wages for long.
do: **Cancel** the family visit and list mortgage, crew costs and confirmed roofing work.
**Save** from each newly paid roof job while both household wages continue.
**Apply** for posted local cabinet inspection work only if pay and day shift fit family bills.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected household loss, lying awake after the children sleep.
S2.quote: I can chase invoices now, but turning a few hours at the table into a full wage needs actual customers.
fieldNote: **Dana** does not confuse 2028 ordering AI with capable hands-on robots around 2031.
She **makes** a move into Greg’s office depend on real paid roofing orders after materials and crew costs.
The **cabinet** inspection fallback requires a posted nearby role with mortgage-covering pay and school-compatible hours.

steps.text: Cancel the planned family visit and list confirmed household and crew costs
Add fresh earnings from paid roofing jobs to savings while wages continue
Apply for posted local cabinet inspection work only if pay and day shift fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years gives the furniture plant time to train a real setter, not just print certificates. AGI can change orders in 2031; capable panel-handling robots follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might lose the edge-bander role at 51 when the robot loaders are good enough. In five years I could learn maintenance or build Greg’s office work, but neither is a wage until somebody pays for it. Our mortgage still arrives every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take a paid machine-setting course in the first year if the plant offers supervised practice and a posted setter opening that pays at least my current wage. After completing it I would apply for that job, and I would keep the edge-bander shift until an offer is signed. From each additional roofing payment after crew costs, Greg and I would put a fixed amount toward the mortgage principal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but there is time to test the course and the roofing accounts. A real pay packet matters more than a course badge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the setter opening never appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would keep this machine job while it lasts and check advertised day-shift operator roles nearby. I would apply if the posted pay covers our mortgage and pickup still works. I would not wait for a vacancy that has never been approved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Greg want you working for him full time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He says yes when his accounts pile up. I would show him what comes in after the crew and van are paid before either of us changes jobs. We have been married long enough to know a roofing desk can be busy and still pay a poor wage.

say: I would **ask** the plant for a paid course attached to an approved setter opening.
The **timing** of office AI and physical panel robots gives me five years to test wages.
think: My **edge-bander** role may shrink around 2034 when I am 51.
**Roofing** paperwork is not a replacement wage until Greg has enough paid jobs.
do: **Complete** paid setter training if supervised and linked to a posted role at current wages.
**Apply** for the posted setter job after training and stay on the bander until offered.
**Pay** extra mortgage principal from new roofing receipts after the crew is covered.
feel: **Anxious** about future work, with time to compare actual pay and course terms.
S3.quote: We have been married long enough to know a roofing desk can be busy and still pay a poor wage.
fieldNote: **Dana** keeps training, application and continuing paid work as separate choices.
The **course** requires supervised paid practice and a real setter opening at her current wage.
**Extra** mortgage payments come from additional roofing receipts after crew and van costs, not from existing savings.

steps.text: Complete paid supervised setter course if a posted role pays current wage
Apply for posted setter job after training and keep bander shifts until offered
Pay extra mortgage principal from additional roofing receipts after crew costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell neighbours that ten years is time to keep apprenticeships and family firms working, if owners show their plans early. I would want the plant to name its robot dates and paid training places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 in 2036 when AGI changes ordering and quotes, and 56 around the 2039 robot date. The children would be older, yet the mortgage might still need both wages. Greg’s roofing business is worth growing only while customers pay for roofs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the edge-bander for now and complete a paid setter course if the plant offers supervised hours and a posted role with my present wage. I would apply for that role after the course; if no paid place appears, I would search separately for posted day-shift machine jobs with mortgage-covering pay and workable pickup. Greg and I would buy a second van from roofing profits only after confirmed orders cover the van costs and our family reserve stays intact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the distant change but secure enough to check each decision. I do not want our children paying for a hasty van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would prove the van can earn its keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Six months of confirmed roof work after paying the crew and materials, plus enough cash for the mortgage if rain stops a week. I would write it out beside the van quote. Greg can argue with the numbers instead of with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the plant to run the roofing office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might, but only after paid roof work leaves enough for my wage and the mortgage over several months. Until then I can do invoices after school pickup. A family firm has to pay the family, not just look busy.

say: I would **ask** the plant for named robot dates and paid training places.
I would **tell** neighbours that family firms need orders, not slogans, before buying new equipment.
think: At 53 in 2036 I **may** still run the bander while order software changes.
At 56 in 2039, **robot** loaders and roofing machines could threaten both wages.
do: **Keep** the bander while checking a paid supervised setter place and posted role.
**Apply** for posted setter work after training, or bill-covering day-shift operator work if no course.
**Buy** a second roofing van only from profits after confirmed orders cover its cost.
feel: **Uneasy** about distant risk, secure enough to test real orders and job terms.
S4.quote: A family firm has to pay the family, not just look busy.
fieldNote: **Dana** prefers firm-led apprenticeship and verified family-business earnings to promises of support without work.
She **separates** the funded setter route from a no-course fallback with its own posted pay and pickup conditions.
A **second** van depends on confirmed roof orders, crew costs, the family reserve and mortgage coverage.

steps.text: Complete paid supervised setter course if offered with posted role at current pay
Apply for posted setter role after training if pay covers mortgage
Apply for posted day-shift operator work if no course wages cover mortgage and pickup
Buy roofing van only from profits after confirmed orders cover costs and reserve remains

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year AGI picture worries me most because panel-handling robots around 2031 could cut my factory hours just as Greg’s roofing orders change. Paid supervised training tied to a real setter vacancy and early notice of the machines would help us keep the mortgage covered.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask factory mothers what time they can collect their children. An operator job with the wrong shift can be as useless as a job with the wrong wage.

headlineQuote: An operator job with the wrong shift can be as useless as a job with the wrong wage.
portrait: **Dana** Schmidt, 43, runs an edge-bander in a cupboard factory and holds a vocational certificate.
She and her **roofer** husband Greg have two school-age children, a mortgage and roughly three months of expenses saved.
She **checks** AI-drafted roofing invoices herself, prefers paid apprenticeships and waits for proven plant changes.
**Possible** cuts to her factory hours make steady disruption anxious, while fast robot change threatens both family wages.
She **weighs** posted setter work and Greg’s business against real wages, day-shift pickup and confirmed customer orders.
biggestWorry: **Fast** AGI could cut her edge-bander hours around 2031 while roofing income also weakens.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid** supervised setter training linked to a posted vacancy and early robot installation dates would help.
